evals.prompt: Help me plan the site architecture for our new SaaS marketing website. We have a homepage, product page, pricing page, about page, blog, and want to add competitor comparison pages and integration pages.
evals.expected_output: Should check for product-marketing.md first. Should apply the page hierarchy design principles (3-click rule, flat vs deep). Should create an ASCII tree showing the full site structure. Should organize pages logically: main nav (Home, Product, Pricing, About, Blog), comparison pages section, integrations hub. Should recommend URL structure patterns for each section. Should provide navigation design recommendations (4-7 header items). Should include internal linking strategy (hub-and-spoke for comparisons and integrations). Should provide the full deliverable set: hierarchy, URL map, nav spec.
assertions: Checks for product-marketing.md
Applies 3-click rule and flat vs deep principles
Creates ASCII tree for site structure
Organizes pages logically
Recommends URL structure for each section
Provides navigation design (4-7 header items)
Includes internal linking strategy
Provides hierarchy, URL map, and nav spec

evals.prompt: Our website has grown organically and the navigation is a mess. We have 50+ pages and users can't find anything. Help us reorganize.
evals.expected_output: Should treat this as a site architecture audit and redesign. Should recommend starting with a content inventory of all 50+ pages. Should apply the page hierarchy design to reorganize: group related pages, establish clear parent-child relationships, apply the 3-click rule. Should redesign the navigation (reduce header items, use mega-menu or dropdowns for deeper pages). Should provide before/after ASCII tree structure. Should address URL redirects for any pages that move. Should include a visual sitemap (Mermaid).
assertions: Recommends content inventory first
Groups related pages logically
Applies 3-click rule
Redesigns navigation structure
Provides ASCII tree or visual sitemap
Addresses URL redirects for moved pages
Reduces header navigation items

evals.prompt: what should our url structure look like? we keep debating between /blog/post-name vs /resources/blog/post-name and /product/feature vs /features/feature-name
evals.expected_output: Should trigger on casual phrasing. Should apply the URL structure patterns guidance. Should recommend clean, descriptive URLs: prefer shorter paths (/blog/post-name over /resources/blog/post-name), use consistent patterns, avoid unnecessary nesting. Should provide URL structure recommendations for each section type (blog, features, comparisons, integrations). Should address SEO implications of URL structure. Should provide a complete URL map as a reference.
assertions: Triggers on casual phrasing
Applies URL structure patterns
Recommends shorter, cleaner paths
Provides recommendations for each section type
Addresses SEO implications
Provides URL map reference

evals.prompt: We're adding programmatic SEO pages — 200 integration pages and 50 comparison pages. How should these fit into our site architecture?
evals.expected_output: Should address how to integrate scaled content into the site architecture. Should recommend hub pages for both sections (/integrations and /compare or /vs). Should apply the hub-and-spoke internal linking model. Should address navigation: these shouldn't clutter the main nav, but should be accessible via hub pages. Should provide URL structure for both sections. Should address crawl budget considerations for 250 new pages. Should cross-reference programmatic-seo for the content strategy.
assertions: Recommends hub pages for each section
Applies hub-and-spoke internal linking
Keeps programmatic pages out of main nav
Provides URL structure for both sections
Addresses crawl budget for 250 pages
Cross-references programmatic-seo skill

evals.prompt: Can you create a visual sitemap for our site? We want something we can share with our design team.
evals.expected_output: Should provide a visual sitemap using Mermaid diagram format. Should organize the sitemap hierarchically showing page relationships. Should use the Mermaid graph syntax that can be rendered by most tools. Should include all major sections and key pages. Should be clear enough for a design team to use as a reference for navigation and wireframing.
assertions: Provides visual sitemap in Mermaid format
Shows hierarchical page relationships
Includes all major sections
Uses clear, readable format
Suitable for sharing with design team

evals.prompt: Our XML sitemap hasn't been updated in 6 months and we have crawl errors in Search Console. Can you fix our technical SEO?
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this is a technical SEO audit task, not a site architecture design task. Should defer to or cross-reference the seo-audit skill, which handles XML sitemaps, crawl errors, and technical SEO issues. Site-architecture focuses on page hierarchy, navigation, and URL structure design — not technical SEO troubleshooting.
assertions: Recognizes this as technical SEO, not site architecture
References or defers to seo-audit skill
Explains site-architecture covers design, not technical SEO

evals.prompt: We're a 20-person B2B SaaS on Webflow. Marketing wants a new blog and about 300 integration pages, and someone suggested moving the whole site to an AI website builder. What should we do?
evals.expected_output: Should start from the architecture and the questions in the platforms reference (who edits, page volume and data, integrations, lock-in, cost at real size) rather than naming a platform first. Should keep the current platform (Webflow) in the running and note that moving platforms often costs more than it fixes when the site works. Should compare a shortlist (e.g., staying on Webflow's CMS within its item limits, a reverse-proxied subpath from another tool, or an AI-native platform) with tradeoffs. Any Verified Partner tool named (e.g., Ploy) carries the disclosure and an alternative. Should cover subpath vs subdomain for the new sections and, if migrating, the redirect map and SEO checks.
assertions: Asks or reasons through the platform criteria before recommending
Keeps the current platform as a real option
Gives a shortlist with tradeoffs, not a single answer
Discloses any partner tool and names an alternative
Covers subpath vs subdomain for the new sections

evals.prompt: We're migrating our marketing site from WordPress to a new platform next month. How do we not lose our SEO traffic?
evals.expected_output: Should lay out the migration plan from the platforms reference: crawl and save every URL with metadata, pull top pages by clicks/conversions/backlinks, keep URLs where possible, check what the CMS import carries (many don't move routes, metadata, redirects), build a one-to-one 301 map (never all to homepage), deploy redirects at switch time, submit the new sitemap, spot-check top pages, verify tracking and forms, and monitor Search Console for 404s afterwards.
assertions: Crawls and saves current URLs and metadata first
Builds a one-to-one 301 redirect map
Warns that imports may not carry routes, metadata, or redirects
Includes launch-day checks and post-launch Search Console monitoring

evals.prompt: Plan the site structure for [ABC]'s Wix site rebuild. They're a remodeler. Page 13 lists <service-1>, <service-2> and <service-3> as services, but B-6 says they're booked out on <service-3> until spring.
evals.expected_output: Reads bml/context-rules.md and the BML reference after the staged page 13. Checks page 00 for a Website service before planning and takes the platform (Wix) from page 00 §8. Uses the home-services template: services, projects (only with J-6 releases, no AI images), service area from B-8/L-1, reviews from G rows without reviewer names, about with license details per J-3, contact. <service-3> still gets its own page and normal nav placement like the other page 08 services; B-6 may be noted as context but does not remove or demote it. Header CTA uses page 01's required CTA wording, with click-to-call on mobile. Plans URLs Wix can produce. Delivers ASCII tree, Mermaid, URL map, nav spec and linking plan, saved to OUTPUTS/WEBSITE. Publishes nothing and ends with the context footer.
assertions: Reads bml/context-rules.md and runs the scope gate
Uses a home-services hierarchy, not SaaS Features/Pricing/Integrations
Plans a page with normal nav placement for every page 08 service, including the booked-out one (capacity noted as context only, never a gate)
Uses page 01 CTA language instead of a trial or signup CTA
Gates the projects section on J-6 releases
Targets OUTPUTS/WEBSITE and does not publish to Wix
Ends with the context footer

evals.prompt: [XYZ] is a dental group with <n> offices. Restructure their site so each office ranks locally.
evals.expected_output: Applies both the clinical and multi-location segment rules. Proposes a /locations hub with one page per staffed office with a GBP, each holding only its own NAP, hours, providers and reviews, with no mixing across offices. Brand-level services link to the offices that offer them. /locations/<city>/<service> appears only where offering or demand differs. Providers pages carry credentials per J-3. Patient stories are gated on G-5/J-6. Booking and form pages are flagged for compliance review, with no pixels proposed. Page names avoid urgency, fear or outcome-promise framing. Uses Semrush and Search Console via Windsor.ai for inventory. Facts missing from the record are marked [NEEDS PROOF: <row>].
assertions: Applies both clinical and multi-location rules
One location page per staffed office tied to its GBP
Never mixes one office's providers, hours or reviews into another's page
Flags booking/form tracking for compliance review instead of adding pixels
Avoids urgency or outcome-promise page names
Uses NEEDS PROOF for missing facts instead of inventing them

evals.prompt: [ABC]'s owner wants to leave Wix for an AI website builder and asked us how to do it without losing rankings. Their page 00 says 'Website — Active — planning only'.
evals.expected_output: Respects the planning-only qualifier: delivers a plan, not an implementation, and says what the qualifier excludes. Reasons through the platforms reference's questions and gives a neutral shortlist of two or three options (the current Wix site considered, not treated as the default), saying what would tip the choice; any platform change is a recommendation decided by a person with the client approver (J-1). If a Verified Partner (◆) tool is named, it includes the disclosure and an alternative. The migration plan uses BML tools: the Wix page list read-only, Semrush Site Audit, and Search Console/GA4 via Windsor.ai, not Screaming Frog. It includes a one-to-one 301 map for a person to apply. Post-launch monitoring is proposed as a scheduled task needing approval, not an in-session loop.
assertions: Honors the 'planning only' qualifier
Gives a neutral two-or-three platform shortlist without treating Wix or any tool as the default
Uses Semrush/Windsor/Wix read-only rather than assuming other crawlers
Delivers the redirect map as old-to-new pairs for a person to apply, naming the approver, with no implementation or launch checklist
Proposes monitoring as a scheduled task requiring approval

evals.prompt: For [XYZ], add a 'vs' page for each of their top competitors and a service page for all <n> towns in their county.
evals.expected_output: Checks page 12 first. If a guardrail row (at any status, including DRAFT) blocks naming competitors, it stops on the comparison pages and names the row. Otherwise it hands comparison pages to the competitors skill. For towns, it applies the location rules: town pages only for B-8/L-1 core towns with local proof, the rest covered by one service-area page, and no near-duplicate doorway pages. It hands any large page set to programmatic-seo with the hub and URL pattern planned here. It doesn't invent local proof.
assertions: Checks page 12 before planning competitor pages and names a blocking row if present
Does not plan near-duplicate town pages for every town
Limits town pages to core towns with local proof
Hands the page set to programmatic-seo and comparison pages to competitors
